Chasmistes liorus, the June sucker endemic to Utah Lake, exhibits a life history tightly coupled to a coldwater thermal regime. Field surveys indicate that incubation proceeds for approximately 9 days [ab = approximately 9 days] at a water temperature of 13 °C [T = 13 °C], after which yolk-sac larvae emerge weighing roughly 0.0042 grams [Wwb = roughly 0.0042 grams]. This modest birth mass, computed from an average egg diameter of 2 millimeters, reflects the energetic constraints of a pelagic spawning strategy where females broadcast small, yolk-laden eggs over gravel substrates. The brief embryonic period is comparable to that of other western catostomids, although the low temperature likely prolongs chorionase activity relative to warmer-water congeners. Following eclosion, the prolarvae remain lecithotrophic, absorbing yolk nutrients before the onset of exogenous feeding.

As juveniles transition to exogenous nutrition, growth trajectories diverge markedly between the sexes, though both ultimately converge on similar asymptotic sizes. Mark-recapture studies have documented a maximum total length of 67 centimeters [Li = 67 centimeters] for the largest recorded adults, a value that positions the June sucker among the larger members of the Catostomidae. This ultimate length corresponds to an asymptotic wet body mass of approximately 3559 grams [Wwi = approximately 3559 grams], as derived from length-mass regressions on field-collected specimens. Such a substantial adult mass likely confers advantages during periodic droughts, when larger individuals can withstand prolonged fasting better than smaller conspecifics.

Sexual maturation in Chasmistes liorus follows a prolonged juvenile phase characteristic of a long-lived, iteroparous freshwater teleost. Puberty is attained between 5 and 7 years after hatching, with a mean age at sexual maturity of approximately 6 years [tp = approximately 6 years] when maintained at a stable thermal regime of 13 °C [T = 13 °C]. At this developmental milestone, the total length at puberty averages 46.5 centimeters [Lp = 46.5 centimeters], representing roughly 70% of the ultimate length. Field observations indicate that first reproduction is not immediate upon reaching gonadal maturity; rather, individuals may delay spawning for another year until sufficient body condition accumulates.

Reproductive output in the June sucker is substantial, reflecting a strategy that balances high fecundity against modest annual survival rates. During a typical spawning event over gravel shoals, individual females release approximately 60000 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = approximately 60000 eggs per clutch], and typically produce one clutch per year [F_R_i = one clutch per year] when measured at 13 °C [T = 13 °C]. This figure is derived from dividing the total seasonal egg complement by the duration of the reproductive period.

Longevity in Chasmistes liorus is among the highest recorded for North American catostomids, with the oldest documented individuals surviving for 44 years [am = 44 years] under the thermal conditions typical of Utah Lake, estimated at 13 °C [T = 13 °C]. This extended lifespan is consistent with a slow life-history pace involving delayed maturation, iteroparous spawning, and relatively low adult natural mortality. The combination of a 44-year lifespan (44 years) [am = 44 years] and a high daily reproductive output yields a lifetime fecundity that can exceed several hundred thousand eggs per female, underscoring the species' capacity for population recovery under favorable environmental conditions at a temperature of 13 °C [T = 13 °C].
